narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 90.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That high estimate placed you in the group considered too risky for admission, even though it is a prediction, not a certainty.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, whereas accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That low standing was the single largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor: at 25.50, it was well below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor: you were again in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, adding further weight toward a fail prediction. These academic indicators outweighed other details such as family income and full-time status.

To improve a future application, focus on strengthening the areas weighted most: seek structured LSAT preparation and retake if advisable, and use academic support and advising to address the class-standing pattern. Consider applying after demonstrating improved academic performance, and ask admissions staff what evidence they would accept.
